title: Collect employees into a `TreeSet<Employee>` sorted by salary using `Collectors.toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)))`.
shortTitle: Collect employees into a TreeSet<Employee> sorted by salary

s1_definition.profdef: `collect(Collectors.toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(comparator)))` gathers elements into a `TreeSet` ordered by the supplied comparator, here salary, keeping the employees sorted and deduplicated by that comparator.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya files employees into a self-sorting drawer ordered by salary, so they stay in salary order automatically.
s1_definition.oneliner: `toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(comparing(salary)))` collects into a salary-sorted set.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `collect(Collectors.toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(comparator)))` gathers elements into a `TreeSet` ordered by the supplied comparator, here salary, keeping the employees sorted and deduplicated by that comparator.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya files employees into a self-sorting drawer ordered by salary, so they stay in salary order automatically.

**One line to remember:** `toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(comparing(salary)))` collects into a salary-sorted set.

sections.s2_technical:
`toCollection(supplier)` lets you choose the exact collection to collect into. Supplying `() -> new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))` creates a TreeSet ordered by salary, so elements are inserted in sorted position and the set stays sorted. The result is a `TreeSet<Employee>` iterable in ascending salary order.

A crucial subtlety: a TreeSet determines equality by the comparator, not by equals. So two employees with the same salary are considered duplicates and only one is kept. That is usually not what you want for a people set, so the comparator must include a tie-breaker like name to keep distinct employees.

The senior nuance is exactly that comparator-based equality: with a salary-only comparator, equal salaries collapse to one element, silently dropping people. I always add a tie-breaker, for example `comparing(salary).thenComparing(id)`, so distinct employees are retained while still sorted by salary. Choosing toCollection over toSet is how I control both the type and the ordering. This comparator-equality pitfall is a classic TreeSet trap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A ranked roster at the National Bank of India must keep employees sorted by salary, with no two distinct employees lost even when salaries tie.

This is exactly what toCollection with a salary comparator plus a tie-breaker does — it sorts by salary and keeps all distinct employees.

The code defines a `RosterService.sortedBySalary method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh 1,000,000, Amit 800,000, Priya 800,000.

Step 1: toCollection creates a TreeSet ordered by salary then name.

Step 2: Amit and Priya both earn 800,000, but the name tie-breaker keeps them distinct — Amit before Priya alphabetically.

Step 3: Rajesh at 1,000,000 sorts after them.

Step 4: Iterating the TreeSet yields Amit, Priya, Rajesh in ascending salary order, all three retained.

```
INFO: Amit : 800000.0
INFO: Priya : 800000.0
INFO: Rajesh : 1000000.0
```

    ▼

sections.s6_takeaway:
To collect employees into a salary-sorted set I use Collectors toCollection with a supplier that creates a TreeSet built on a salary comparator. toCollection lets me choose the exact collection type, and the TreeSet keeps the employees in ascending salary order as they are inserted, iterating in that order. At the National Bank of India this backs a ranked roster.

The critical trap I always call out is that a TreeSet decides equality by its comparator, not by the elements' equals method. So if I use a salary-only comparator, two employees with the same salary are treated as equal and one is silently dropped. That is almost never what I want for a set of people, so I add a tie-breaker — comparing by salary and then by name or id — which keeps distinct employees while still sorting by salary.

The senior point I stress is exactly that comparator-equality pitfall. Choosing toCollection over toSet gives me control over both the concrete type and the ordering, but with a TreeSet I must make the comparator total enough to distinguish genuinely different elements, otherwise the set quietly loses data. A salary comparator with a name tie-breaker gives me a sorted roster that retains every distinct employee.
